html:
On 30 September 2005 the Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten printed twelve cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad. Months later they set off protests across the Muslim world.

The editors said they wanted to test self-censorship about Islam. Many Muslims saw the drawings as an insult, since images of the Prophet are widely forbidden and one showed him with a bomb in his turban. In early 2006 Danish missions in Damascus and Beirut were set on fire, goods from Denmark were boycotted, and more than two hundred people died in riots.

The crisis became a symbol of the clash between free speech and religious feeling in Europe. It hardened Danish debate on immigration. The cartoonists faced death threats, and similar drawings led later to the attack on Charlie Hebdo in Paris in 2015.
sum: On 30 September 2005 the Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten printed twelve cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad. Months later they set off protests across the Muslim world.
